articles.headline: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges
keyFacts: AI startup Fal raised $1.3 billion in a funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, reaching a valuation of $16 billion, Bloomberg reported.
The funding follows soaring demand for AI inference services, with Fal having surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, according to Bloomberg.
Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur and Gorkem Yurtseven, according to the company.
body: Fal, a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported.
The startup announced its Series E & F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.)

The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open-source models. Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg’s report noted.

Companies providing inference services, including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal, have also been growing rapidly and raising large funding rounds at higher valuations. But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials.
Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon.

articles.headline: Netflix producing new Dana White documentary reportedly greenlit during talks for UFC rights
keyFacts: Page Six reported that Netflix quietly began producing a documentary about UFC executive Dana White last year.
The documentary project reportedly emerged during Netflix talks to buy UFC broadcast rights, which ultimately went to Paramount.
Page Six reported that the untitled documentary about Dana White will be released early next year.
body: Screen grab: UFC There is never a bad time for a Dana White story.
The brash sports entrepreneur continues to expand his influence, not only through the continued popularity of the UFC but also his impact as a political actor and businessman.

It turns out that last year, according to Page Six , Netflix quietly began producing a documentary on White. The project reportedly came out of the streamer’s interest in buying UFC broadcast rights , which ultimately went to Paramount on a deal worth more than $1 billion annually .
The doc will be directed by famed documentarian Gotham Chopra, who Page Six notes was working on a separate project about the city of Las Vegas that seemingly morphed into this White story.

The reported development process of the White doc mirrors that of 2024’s Vince McMahon series, Mr. McMahon . Executive produced by Bill Simmons , Mr. McMahon earned Awful Announcing’s year-end award as the best documentary of that year , despite being executive produced by McMahon and the WWE after Netflix bought rights to Monday night Raw .

Whether White has oversight over the reported Netflix doc is unclear. The UFC boss is quick to mix it up with the media and isn’t afraid to go on offense to control the message around his business, but very little is off limits with White. Done correctly, it is not impossible to imagine a White doc cutting through, even if he is involved in its production.

Recently, Netflix exec Gabe Spitzer acknowledged the streamer had greenlit too many “league-follow” docuseries in the mold of Drive To Survive . Spitzer added that Netflix is working to reimagine its approach to sports docs at a time when genuine access is hard to come by and the industry is running thinner on compelling subjects.
Page Six reports the untitled White doc will drop early next year.

articles.headline: MLB backed Mark Teixeira's congressional campaign before his Giants' Pride Night criticism
keyFacts: The Office of the Commissioner of Major League Baseball PAC donated $5,000 to former MLB player Mark Teixeira's congressional campaign on June 8, 2026.
Teixeira forcefully condemned the San Francisco Giants' Pride Night and criticized MLB for warning players who protested the event by writing Bible verses on their hats.
Federal Election Commission filings confirmed the donation, while MLB did not respond to requests for comment regarding the contribution and subsequent controversy.
body: The Office of the Commissioner of Major League Baseball PAC donated $5,000 to former All-Star Mark Teixeira's congressional campaign on June 8, 2026, according to Federal Election Commission filings USA TODAY Sports reviewed. Teixeira's campaign confirmed receipt on June 12. That evening, the San Francisco Giants hosted a Pride Night event, which Teixeira forcefully condemned in the following weeks.

Teixeira, running as a Republican in Texas' 21st District, criticized a warning MLB sent to some Giants players who protested the evening by writing bible verses on their Pride Night hats. MLB said the players violated league uniform policies. Teixeira called the warning an attempt to "silence" Christian athletes.

"I played in the major leagues for 14 years," Teixeira told Fox News on June 30. "We play 162 games a year, we don't have these conversations. We don't take political stances. It's a hard job playing baseball and bringing something like a pride night and forcing players to wear a cap. Whether that was the rule or not, that's what it looked like."
MLB did not respond to USA TODAY Sports' request for comment.
More: 5 sports figures running for office in 2026 election. Who's funding them?

The league has a long history of political contributions and has previously requested candidates return donations. In 2018, MLB requested the return of $5,000 it gave to the campaign of Mississippi republican Cindy Hyde-Smith . That request came two weeks after she appeared in a video joking about attending "public hangings."
After the controversy, Manfred said the league office would review all donations before "any checks are cut."

"It's hard when you have an organization as large as ours, with as many issues that are impacted by the political process, to be completely out," Manfred said after the Hyde-Smith donation. "We are very cognizant, however, that in today's world, those kind of donations run the risk of being controversial with segments of our society."

articles.headline: Someone Just Figured Out How To Recruit A Previously Unrecruitable Party Member In A Nearly 30-Year-Old RPG
keyFacts: A fan named Azekura discovered that a tenth party member, Lilith Aileron, can be legitimately recruited in the original 1997 PS1 game Tales of Destiny.
Original producer Jun Toyoda apologized on X, explaining that developers intended to cut Lilith due to debugging constraints but failed to remove her fully.
Toyoda stated that recruiting Lilith in the original Japanese version causes a game softlock that requires players to switch to a later version to continue.
body: Tales of Destiny is a PS1 RPG originally released in Japan in December 1997. While quietly beloved by some fans, it’s historically been one of the more obscure Tales games due to never getting released on modern consoles and its PS2 ports only coming out in Japan. No modern remakes yet.
For years, fans have assumed there were a total of nine possible party members in the original game. Yesterday, nearly 30 years after the original release, someone found a tenth.

Lilith Aileron, frying-pan wielder and younger sister of protagonist Stahn, is officially, legitimately recruitable in the original Tales of Destiny, and it was onlyÂ just now discovered. And I cannot emphasize enough how batshit this find is.

For one, the person who found it, Azekura, is a longtime Tales fan and administrator of Majestic Fantasian, a Japanese Tales fansite. The process for recruitment has since been corroborated by multiple other individuals on both the English and Japanese versions of the game, and has also been corroborated by one of the original developers posting on Twitter/X, who apologized because her recruitment (which is a wildly convoluted process) apparently softlocks the game in the original edition but can be salvaged by moving to later versions. I’m floored.

But in the original PS1 version, it was just always assumed that she had been removed at the last minute for some unknown reason, and no one really followed up until now.

But probably the most obvious reason no one ever found Lilith’s recruitment requirements is that they seem to be pretty convoluted. As I write this, the actual list of rules still isn’t fully known. Azekura documented what they believe to be the requirements, but it’s possible some of them aren’t actually required and testers are working right now to figure out which things are and aren’t important. You have to save before you enter a town, shut down the game, and then run it on the “BEST” version to continue.

Via machine translation, he said: “It’s amazing that you managed to find a way to recruit Lilith as a companion. articles.headline: Itch.io adds a filter for games with gen AI disclosures
keyFacts: Game hosting site Itch.io announced that it is adding filters for AI-generated content.
Applying the No AI filter reduced the number of visible projects from over 1.77 million to under 425,000.
Itch.io policy prohibits uploading excessive amounts of AI-generated content and treats those actions as spam.
body: Itch.io adds a filter for games with gen AI disclosures
Your turn, Steam.

Game hosting site Itch.io announced that it is adding filters for AI-generated content. There is now a "No AI" option in the menu when browsing. For games, applying the filter today took the number of projects shown from more than 1.77 million to less than 425,000. The filter has also been added to its search feature and other spots where, in the company's own words, it was "critically lacking."

The platform has policies about use of generative AI on the books. Itch.io doesn't allow "uploading excessive amounts of automatically generated or AI-generated content," and said it will treat those actions as spam. It also asks creators to disclose use of generative AI when appropriate, but doesn't state whether there are penalties for not using the tag where it's merited. The rules haven't stopped AI slop from appearing (and disappearing) from the service. Itch.io is also a popular site for running game jams, and those can take widely differing stances toward AI use, from being outright prohibited to being the point.

Steam, a much larger gaming marketplace, also has rules governing disclosures for generative AI use, but there's not currently a way to filter them out in the store. Even if these platforms rely on self-reporting, it's still nice to have the option to avoid the slop when you want to.

articles.headline: Jason Wilcox backed Russell Martin as future Man United manager in shock revelation
keyFacts: Manchester United director of football Jason Wilcox previously earmarked Russell Martin as a surprise managerial candidate in 2024.
The Athletic reported that Wilcox tipped Martin while brainstorming potential successors during Erik ten Hag’s tenure.
Wilcox remains an admirer of Martin, though United's current board is split between Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann.
body: Manchester United director of football Jason Wilcox earmarked Russell Martin as a surprise managerial target for them in 2024.
The Red Devils currently find themselves at a potential managerial crossroads with Michael Carrick running out of time to turn things around.
Once touted as a potential Man United manager, Russell Martin currently manages in League One with Leicester Getty
United are languishing in 16th place in the Premier League and without a win in nine games after a 2-0 defeat to Chelsea .
While Carrick has been given a stay of execution for now, this isn’t expected to extend for much longer if results continue to disappoint.
Speculation is already rife over who could succeed the United legend if he is sacked, and talkSPORT understands the club’s board are split over whether to hire Eddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmann .
But there could be another candidate in the back of Wilcox’s mind, if he chooses to revisit a past option.
Russell Martin recommendation
According to the Athletic, under-fire United chief Wilcox previously tipped current Leicester boss Martin as a possible future manager when Erik ten Hag‘s position was under threat in 2024.
While Ten Hag ultimately kept his job after FA Cup glory the 2023/24 season, Wilcox had been tasked with brainstorming potential successors to the Dutchman.
Wilcox is said to have pushed for Martin – who he appointed as Southampton boss in his previous role 2023.
The English coach’s stock was high after guiding the Saints to the Premier League via the Championship play-offs in the 2023/24 season.
The Athletic report that Wilcox accepted that Martin, at that stage of his career, would not be suitable for the United job but still earmarked him as a manager to keep tabs on.
Ten Hag ultimately held onto his job for another few months before Ruben Amorim was preferred as his successor in November 2024.
Carrick is facing a race against time to hold onto his job AFP
Wilcox is yet to have his desired impact after over two years at Man United Getty
Since then, Martin has endured a tough run of things in his managerial career, starting with his sacking at Southampton .
After guiding them back to the top-flight, he was relieved of his duties just four months into their return after losing 13 of their first 16 matches.
A disastrous spell at Rangers followed in 2025 where Martin saw his tenure cut short after 17 games, winning just five times.
The 40-year-old took charge of Leicester in the summer, and is now climbing up the League One table after a difficult start .

While it now looks unlikely United will turn to Martin should they opt to change manager, Wilcox is understood to be a fan of his tactical understanding, strong vision of playing style and leadership skills.
This is believed to be in line with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe ‘s views, who is keen for the club to follow a clear game model.
The highlight of Martin’s managerial career came at Southampton as he masterminded their return to the Premier League
Ratcliffe urged to make ‘ruthless’ call
While Wilcox’s earmarking of Martin may get Ratcliffe’s seal of approval, United’s sporting director remains unpopular among fans.

The team’s board have faced criticism over the club’s demise since their appointments following INEOS’ takeover in February 2024, while Wilcox recently came in for a stinging attack by defender Lisandro Martinez over a lack of recruitment in the summer.

And now, United fan and pundit Flex has joined criticism of the United chief, insisting the club should instead look to overhaul their board as the prospect of sacking a third manager in two years looms.
He urged owner Ratcliffe to replace Wilcox, and claimed his previous work in the Manchester City academy and as Southampton director of football do not make him qualified for his current role.

On talkSPORT’s ‘The S Word’, Flex said: “You employed Jason Wilcox. You employed Omar Berrada. These are your guys. You made a footballing department that is failing. I want the same ruthlessness to say, ‘Jason, see ya.’
He continued: “He should never have got there. Jason Wilcox is a seasoned pro at academy level.
Wilcox’s credentials and his recommendation of Martin have been called into question Getty
“He did a fantastic job at City for what it’s worth with the academy players. Yes, he found Cole Palmer , Jadon Sancho , Morgan Rogers , [Romeo] Lavia etc – youngsters.

“Then you went to Southampton with Russell Martin and his best bit of work is going on – this sort of 25 game [unbeaten run] in the Championship with Martin and getting to the Prem. That’s his best work.
“And then once he got to the Prem, we all know how that ended up and where Russell Martin’s gone since. So how does that correlate to – I know can run Manchester United?”
Flex then ridiculed the recent revelations about Wilcox highlighting Martin as a potential future appointment at Old Trafford.
He joked: “He put his name forward after Ten Hag. Do you mean Russell Crowe? Do you mean Russell Westbrook?
“What do you mean, Russell Martin? What do you mean? He can be the manager. What are you talking about?”

articles.headline: The Elder Scrolls 6 is still a long way off, Bethesda warns: 'It'll be some time before we're ready to share more'
keyFacts: Bethesda revealed the subtitle and location of The Elder Scrolls 6 as Sentinel in Hammerfell.
Bethesda warned that it will be some time before the studio is ready to share more information about the game.
Journalist Jason Schreier stated that the game is still more than two years away from release.
body: You might be thinking, if you're the optimistic sort, that today's official unveiling of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel means that wheels are turning and things are happening and you're going to be off to Hammerfell soon—or at the very least, learning more about what's coming in Bethesda's next big RPG. Alas, in a follow-up post on social media, the studio made it clear that you shouldn't start holding your breath just yet.

"Thank you for 40 years of shared memories," Bethesda wrote. "We can't wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it'll be some time before we're ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you."

Thank you for 40 years of shared memories. We can’t wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it’ll be some time before we’re ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you.
— @bethesdastudios.com (@bethesdastudios.com.bsky.social) 2026-11-03T19:25:45.598Z

"Some time" is obviously not a defined span, but I find that generally speaking it's a nicer, more politic way of saying "long time"—for instance, you could say it's been "some time" since Bethesda first announced the Elder Scrolls 6, and yeah, that's true. It was also eight freakin' years ago, and we've heard basically nothing since.

That is, very roughly, the same amount of time Bethesda needed to make the first Elder Scrolls game, Arena, as well as Daggerfall, Morrowind, the Morrowind expansions Tribunal and Bloodmoon, and the spinoff games Battlespire and Redguard. If you're (relatively) new to the series, eight years represents the span between Oblivion and The Elder Scrolls Online, a stretch interspersed by Skyrim and five major expansions: Knights of the Nine and Shivering Isles for Oblivion, and Dawnguard, Hearthfire, and Dragonborn for Skyrim.

Of course, Bethesda's had other things on the go over the past eight years too. Todd Howard said shortly after The Elder Scrolls 6 reveal that it was in pre-production, while Starfield was in full production. Starfield was Bethesda's top priority in the years leading up to its 2023 release; Howard later said that they'd just wanted to answer the fan question (are you making a new Elder Scrolls?) that came up every time they announced something else, like Starfield.
"Just pretend we didn't announce it," he joked. "Doesn't exist. No one's heard a word."

How long Sentinel will take to get from here to launch is anybody's guess, although Bloomberg's Jason Schreier said on Bluesky that it's "still more than two years away." When questioned about his prediction, Schreier asserted that it's not a prediction at all, and that he knows "the time frame the game is targeting."

articles.headline: Jeremiyah Love's difficult rookie season takes another hit with trip to injured reserve
keyFacts: Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love is placed on injured reserve with a high ankle sprain and will miss 4 to 5 weeks.
The injury occurred during the first half of Sunday's overtime win over the Cowboys after he was tackled by multiple defenders.
The Cardinals will rely more on Tyler Allgeier while Love is out of the lineup.
body: Bad luck would be better than the luck Jeremiyah Love has had this season. The Cardinals' rookie running back is heading to injured reserve after sustaining a high ankle sprain during Sunday's overtime win over the Cowboys. Love will be out for 4-5 weeks.

This is Love's second ankle injury of the season. His first one was sustained during the preseason. Sunday's injury took place during the first half when Love was tackled by multiple Cowboys defenders.
In six games, Love has rushed for 268 yards and a touchdown and is averaging only 3.5 yards per carry. He has 11 catches and one receiving touchdown, too.

Ironically, Love's best performance so far was against the 49ers, one of the league's best teams. He ran for 90 yards on 21 carries and also caught each of his five targets for a touchdown in a 36-30 loss.

With Love out, the Cardinals will lean more on Tyler Allgeier, who leads Arizona with 323 yards on the ground. Formerly Bijan Robinson's backup in Atlanta, Allgeier amassed 191 total yards and two touchdowns in Sunday's win over Dallas.

articles.headline: Manchester United v Roma: Champions League – live
keyFacts: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick faces a crucial Champions League match against Roma while his team sits 17th in the Premier League.
Roma is giving a debut to 28-year-old third-choice goalkeeper Devis Vásquez for the fixture.
According to the article, Carrick has until the final whistle against Aston Villa on Sunday to show he can lead the club forward.
body: Michael Carrick: “A big challenge, it’s what you expect. They’ve had a very good start to the season. We want to be in this competition to challenge ourselves against good teams. It’s a big night for us.
“We have to pick a team, we’ve got good players. We’ve made a decision for tonight.
“We’ve got some really good midfielders with different strengths. We think it’s a good time to put Kobbie back in with the attributes him and Baleba have.”
The great John Brewin wrote about how Manchester United have become unmanageable.

Busby and Ferguson built the club around themselves, possessing the charisma to convince others that theirs was the path to follow. Carrick, an insider, a club man, is falling victim to the same isolation as his predecessors in failure. Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez going off-piste in TV interviews to depth charge Carrick were actually following club tradition. With glamour comes decadence, the faded grandeur that has so often chased a United manager out the door.
Bit of fun among the team news … Martinez is dropped, allowing us all to guess how the United back four will start off. I feel Yoro deserves a go at centre-back but I will almost certainly be wrong.
Roma are giving a debut to third-choice goalkeeper Devis Vásquez, who is a 28-year-old who once had a loan at Sheffield Wednesday.

Ayden Heaven was put up for the pre-match interview – don’t worry he did not say anything on note. The Amazon pundits are perplexed that the young defender forced to face the cameras, with Ashley Young and Wayne Rooney wanting someone more senior to take responsibility.

Is this the day Manchester United finally turn their season around and save Michael Carrick’s job? Probably not. The manager is eagerly looking forward to this game despite not winning in nine, sitting 17th in the Premier League and coming into this clash with Roma off the back of two Champions League defeats. Life is not easy for Carrick because he has not fit left-back nor a decent striker available to him, so what can Big Sir Jim really expect?

Carrick, if we are being honest, has until the final whistle on Sunday - when Aston Villa are in town - to show he can lead United forward. Anything other than two wins this week will almost certainly seal his fate. There were promising signs against Chelsea but that soon unravelled.
At the very least, Carrick fronts up amid the misery. Those above him say absolutely nothing but must also fear for their futures after a desperate season thus far.

body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- A senior Iranian figure on Tuesday cast doubt on diplomatic efforts to broker a peace deal with the U.S., calling the Trump administration's response to the latest proposal "not convincing" and insisting that Iran's demands, including for a halt to fighting on all fronts in the Middle East, must be met if the Strait of Hormuz is to reopen.
- American forces near the strait on Monday, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, in response to an apparent Iranian attack targeting a U.S. aircraft.
- President Trump said on the eve of that a deal with Iran to end the still "could happen," insisting Tehran "wants a settlement, as soon as possible."
Saudis intercept drone over eastern part of country
The Saudi-led coalition intercepted a drone over the eastern part of the country on Tuesday evening, according to spokesman Col. Turki Al-Malki.

The one-way attack drone was the second to be intercepted by coalition forces on Tuesday. An earlier drone was intercepted near the holy city of Mecca, though Houthi forces quickly denied the accusation. The Houthis have said publicly they will not target holy sites like Mecca.
There were no further details on the drone intercepted over the eastern part of Saudi Arabia, but the region is the hub of oil production in the country.

The headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's biggest oil company, are located in the eastern city of Dammam. Those headquarters, as well as the airport in Dammam, have been targeted multiple times by the Iran-backed Houthis. The airport, King Fahd International Airport, was targeted yesterday, the Houthis claimed.
Asian Cup soccer tournament latest sporting event in Saudi Arabia to be postponed due to war

The 2027 Asian Cup soccer tournament has been delayed almost a year in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country Saudi Arabia, becoming the biggest sports event to be postponed amid the conflict in the Middle East.

The Asian Football Confederation issued a statement Tuesday that after consultations with Saudi organizers it decided to push the start of its marquee continental championship back from Jan. 7 to Dec. 23.
The decision came to seem likely after developments in recent weeks raised questions over whether the 2034 World Cup host nation is currently safe enough for a major international soccer tournament.

Several major sporting events have been postponed or canceled in Saudi Arabia due to Houthi attacks, including the Women's Tennis Association Finals, which were moved from Riyadh to Indian Wells, California, next week; and Netflix's Six Kings Slam tennis event, which was moved from late October to late December. Saudi Arabia's Formula 1 race was also canceled for the 2026 season back in April.
One exception is World Wrestling Entertainment, which will still be holding its Crown Jewel event in Riyadh this weekend.
CBS/AP
Higher oil prices boost Saudi Aramco profits despite disruption from Houthi attacks

The majority state-owned Saudi Aramco, the largest oil company in the world, on Tuesday reported a 35% increase in third-quarter net profit as earnings were boosted by higher oil prices and the sale of its stake in a Malaysian refining and petrochemical company.

Net profit rose to $36.3 billion from $26.9 billion in the year-earlier quarter. Adjusted net profit, which leaves out the sale of a stake in PRefChem to Malaysian state oil company Petronas, rose 9% to $31.2 billion.
The company also benefitted from high profit margins at its refineries turning crude into usable products such as diesel fuel.

Saudi Aramco sold its oil for an average of $95.20 a barrel during the quarter, compared to $70.10 in the year-before quarter, the company said in a news release. Oil prices surged after the outbreak of the Iran war due to disruption of supply and uncertainty about the course of the conflict.

After the war began, Saudi Aramco was able to use its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to maintain a significant share of its oil exports despite disruption of tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz due to the risk of Iranian attack. The pipeline was attacked Sept. 10 but has since resumed flows.

Saudi oil is now also being transported through the strait using a U.S.-protected corridor near the coast of Oman. Exports have continued despite attacks on Aramco facilities by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
AP/CBS
Islamic Revolutionary Guard says Iran will determine "time and conditions for ending the enemy's attacks"

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Tuesday that the country's armed forces and leadership would determine "the time and conditions for ending the enemy's attacks," after the U.S. carried out what American officials described to CBS News as limited, defensive strikes against Iranian targets on Monday.

In a statement conveyed by the Fars News agency, which is linked with the IRGC, the powerful paramilitary force said orders from Iran's supreme leader had been conveyed to senior military commanders, "in line with 'maximum deterrence' as our top priority, with full force, and we will not hesitate for a moment in implementing it."
The statement did not reveal any clear plans by Iran to retaliate for the latest U.S. strikes.
Senior Iranian official casts doubt on progress toward deal, calls U.S. response to demands "not convincing"

Senior Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei said Tuesday that the U.S. response to "Iran's rights and demands was not convincing," suggesting ongoing efforts by mediators Qatar and Pakistan to broker an agreement between Washington and Tehran still had significant hurdles to overcome.

"America's response to Iran's rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them; only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened," Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran, said in a post on X.

Senior figures in the Iranian regime have stressed for weeks that any agreement with the U.S. to end the war would require Washington to meet demands including a complete cessation of hostilities not only in the Persian Gulf, but in Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, as well as lifting the U.S. blockade of Iran's ports and unfreeing Iranian financial assets held outside the country.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baqaei told reporters later Tuesday that Iran was "not afraid of diplomacy," provided that it was used to "safeguard the interests of the Iranian nation and prevent the escalation of insecurity in the region."

"Given the United States' record of violating previous agreements, we participate in any diplomatic process with the utmost caution and complete distrust," Baqaei said. "Reaching any understanding is conditional on an unequivocal commitment to stopping the war on all fronts, including Lebanon."
U.K. navy agency says attack hit small Indian-crewed vessel in Strait of Hormuz

The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Tuesday that it was "aware of a report by the Indian Government of an attack on an Indian crewed Dhow whilst sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz," seemingly confirming a strike that killed at least one mariner earlier in the day, but clarifying that it was a small vessel, not a large cargo ship.
Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said earlier that the MSV Al Jusufi, which he described as a cargo vessel, had 14 Indian seafarers on board when it was attacked.

"While 13 crew members safely evacuated and were rescued by the Omani Coast Guard, I am deeply saddened to report that one of our seafarers, Gandhar Nahim Ajij from Gujarat, tragically succumbed to his injuries," Sonowal said in a statement on social media.

No one immediately claimed responsibility for the strike, but Iran has attacked numerous cargo ships and tankers in recent months that it accuses of using unauthorized shipping lanes in the south of the Strait of Hormuz, which the U.S. government and military claims are safe and open to commercial traffic.
Trump tells Fox News U.S. aid for Israel worth $4 billion per year to end by 2027
President Trump told Fox News on Tuesday morning that , which he said is worth $4 billion per year, would end by the end of this year.

Mr. Trump gave little detail on the announcement, which appeared to refer to longstanding U.S. military support for Israel, but he said the end of the aid arrangement had been agreed in advance with Prime Minister .

"Netanyahu and I, we made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping, and they're fine with it, because, you know, they've become a very successful country. They don't need it," Mr. Trump told Fox in a phone interview. "We've already agreed that by the end of this year, we won't be paying Israel. Now, we'll help Israel if they need it, you know. They've been a great ally."

U.S. support for Israel in American politics for many years, but the level of military aid in particular has become more hotly debated in Washington since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack that sparked the war in Gaza.

It was in the wake of that war that Israel and the U.S. jointly launched the war against Iran, which has pushed gas and oil prices to record levels over the last eight months, bringing huge pressure on Mr. Trump's Republican party ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections.
Netanyahu told CBS' 60 Minutes earlier this year that he wanted to phase out U.S. military aid to Israel, as he has said on various occasions.

Mr. Trump acknowledged to Fox on Monday that his announcement came after left-wing politicians had used the issue as asking: "Why should we suffer the slings" from Democratic candidates when Israel doesn't need the aid.
Qatar reportedly expects feedback from U.S. and Iran on latest peace proposal within 36 hours

Qatari mediators expect feedback from Iranian and U.S. negotiators on new ideas aimed at getting both sides closer to a deal to end the war within 36 hours, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing an official briefed on the talks.
"The mediators came up with a new suggestion to move the process along, and it's currently being studied by the two sides," the official told Reuters.

Efforts to reach a deal to prevent a return to fighting between Iran and the U.S. have ramped up recently. President Trump has said he is still open to an agreement, but he has also threatened to resume major U.S. strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections.
On the eve of the U.S. elections, Mr. Trump again expressed hope that an agreement could still be reached, claiming Tehran wanted a settlement "as soon as possible."
Iranian officials declared Monday that the ball "is in the U.S. court," and they said Iran's core demands to end the war would not be altered.
Iran "retains the right to legitimate self-defense" after U.S. strikes, senior official says

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tuesday that Tehran reserved the right to self-defense after the U.S. carried out what officials described to CBS News as limited, defensive strikes on the Iranian island of Qeshm in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The Islamic Republic of Iran retains the right to legitimate self-defense until the military aggression has been completely and permanently brought to an end," Gharibabadi was quoted as saying by Iran's ISNA news agency.
The U.S. military on Iranian targets Monday after the country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired at an American aircraft, a senior U.S. official told CBS News.
CBS/AFP
Qatari mediators remain hopeful of deal
Qatar said on Tuesday it remained hopeful that an interim deal could be reached between the United States and Iran as both sides review proposals put forward by mediators.
In recent days, diplomatic efforts have been underway to prevent renewed fighting after the United States threatened major new strikes, though President Trump signalled diplomatic progress with Iran.

"Both parties remain committed to the negotiation process; as we mentioned, we are facilitating the real-time exchange of proposals between them," Qatar's Foreign Ministry Spokesman Majed Al Ansari told reporters.
Both sides "are currently reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented," he added.
"We remain hopeful that there is still a chance for a deal to take place," he said, adding Doha was working "towards an interim deal".
CBS/AFP
1 killed after cargo vessel struck near Strait of Hormuz
An India-flagged cargo vessel was struck by an "unidentified aerial object" off Oman, killing one Indian crew member, New Delhi said Tuesday.
Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said the tanker MSV Al Jusufi had 14 Indian seafarers on board when it was attacked.

"While 13 crew members safely evacuated and were rescued by the Omani Coast Guard, I am deeply saddened to report that one of our seafarers, Gandhar Nahim Ajij from Gujarat, tragically succumbed to his injuries," Sonowal said in a statement on social media.
India is one of the largest contributors of sailors to merchant shipping worldwide, with more than 320,000 active seafarers in 2025, according to the shipping ministry.
Several of its mariners have been killed in attacks in the Strait of Hormuz since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.
India's foreign ministry has repeatedly condemned attacks on commercial vessels, calling for unimpeded and safe navigation through international waters.
U.S. launches limited defensive strikes at Iranian targets near Strait of Hormuz, multiple U.S. officials say
Multiple U.S. officials told CBS News on Monday evening that American forces launched what they described as limited defensive strikes at Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz.
One senior military official said the strikes were directed at Qeshm Island in southern Iran and came in response to Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps firing upon a U.S. aircraft.
The Wall Street Journal first reported on the strikes on Monday.
Trump says a deal with Iran "could happen"

President Trump on Monday signaled progress in talks with Iran to avoid a return to war, as Tehran said "intensive" exchanges were underway while offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions.
A deal with Tehran "could happen," Mr. Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, a day before crucial midterm elections. He added that "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible."
Vice President JD Vance separately said that both he and Mr. Trump were optimistic about securing an agreement.
"We've certainly made some progress. We'll see if we can make some more," Vance told reporters on Monday.
Oil prices, sent rocketing by Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz energy corridor, plunged by more than 7% on Monday on optimism over a possible end to the eight-month-old conflict.
Mr. Trump also pointed to tumbling oil prices in his social media post.
Trump says he hopes war with Iran does not affect Americans "when they go into the voting booth"
President Trump said he hopes the war with Iran doesn't affect voters "when they go into the voting booth."
Mr. Trump mentioned Iran multiple times on Monday during his final scheduled remarks at the ahead of , saying "it's not a war."

"We had a war with, and you know, I don't know if you even call it a war because we haven't been doing any fighting for months," he said. "I hope people realize that when they go into the voting booth because we had to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon."
Tehran residents flock to cafes seeking refuge
Iranians are flocking to stylish cafes in the capital, as they look for respite from soaring inflation and the specter of renewed war with the U.S.
"Cafes offer a chance to unwind, to escape the stress of exorbitant prices, war and anxiety-inducing news," said Mitra Alipour, celebrating her birthday at a coffee shop in Tehran.
Since the start of the Middle East conflict, triggered in late February by U.S.-Israeli airstrikes, "everything has become more expensive," the 28-year-old told AFP.
She regrets that she can no longer travel or afford a new phone, but she can at least get a coffee.
"How do I know if I'll still be able to afford it next year? So I tell myself I'll make the most of it and treat myself, while I still can," she added.
In downtown Tehran, cafes are constantly packed — a striking sight for a country grappling with Western sanctions and an economic slump exacerbated by the war.
Washington has imposed sanctions on Tehran since the 1979 Islamic Revolution toppled the U.S.-backed shah, and more recently has applied further economic pressure.
Yet upscale cafes near shopping malls stocked with Western products remain a common sight along Fereshteh Street, in the city's north.
As night falls, groups of young people and couples head to cafes to unwind and socialize, just meters from Valiasr Avenue, known as the Champs-Elysees of Tehran.
Headscarves are less conspicuous among women in these fashionable neighborhoods, despite compulsory hijab rules introduced after the revolution established clerical rule.
Another vessel struck near Strait of Hormuz, maritime monitor says
Another vessel was struck by an "unknown projectile" near the Strait of Hormuz, according to a report Monday by the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center, or UKMTO, a maritime security agency.

The strike happened Sunday in an area about nine nautical miles off the coast of Lima, Oman, UKMTO said. It caused a hole to form on the starboard side of the vessel, although all crew members were reported safe by its captain, according to the agency.
"Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO, whilst authorities investigate," it said.
Netanyahu is pressing Trump to attack Iran after the midterms, officials say

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for another wave of strikes on Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S., according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter, each of whom spoke with the Associated Press. Their comments followed an earlier report from Axios, which cited sources who said Netanyahu had pushed for President Trump to strike Iran during a call between the two leaders over the weekend, but Mr. Trump wanted to let the negotiations play out.

The two regional officials told AP that diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials. Both officials said the mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports.

They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials.

One official said Netanyahu was working with senior officials in the U.S. administration to persuade Mr. Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign and that the president does not appear to have made a decision.

Other U.S. allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying it would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved.
That official wasn't authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Mr. Trump's discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call.
CBS/AP
Iran VP says indirect exchanges with U.S. point to recognition of Tehran's "victory"
Iran's vice president said on Monday that exchanges with the U.S. via mediators indicated Washington's recognition of Tehran's "victory" in the Middle East war, Iranian state media reported.

"Our enemy failed to achieve any of its objectives in the last two wars. Even today, although the United States, driven by its own goals and concerns regarding domestic public opinion, is engaging in various maneuvers, the messages conveyed to Iran through intermediaries point to an acknowledgment of our victory," said Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref, according to IRNA state news agency.
Oil prices drop roughly 7% ahead of U.S. midterm elections
Oil prices sank around 7% on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the U.S., as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.

Earlier, Axios outlet reported that Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks, in the highest-level move from the Trump administration in months.
Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, chief analyst at Global Risk Management, told AFP that her organization believes such signals from the administration "may be tactical" ahead of the midterms.
"Meanwhile, attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz continue [and] we maintain our higher-for-longer outlook for energy prices," Rasmussen said.

But share prices of energy majors have dropped, while many other sectors were boosted by the cooling fuel costs. Stocks got a lift from sharp drops in oil prices, which headed back down in their latest yo-yo move on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global industry to return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 7.4% to $105.03.
The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $70 and $120 per barrel since just before the war began, and it's been quick to reverse direction.
AP/AFP
Houthi spokesperson says Saudi coalition launched more than 100 strikes since Sunday

Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, a military spokesperson for the Iran-backed Houthis, said Monday that the Saudi coalition fighting the rebel group in Yemen had launched more than 100 airstrikes over the course of the last day.

"Saudi warplanes launched 109 airstrikes over the past 24 hours," the spokesperson said in a statement shared on X. The strikes targeted the Yemeni provinces of Saada, Taiz, Lahj, Al-Jawf, and Hodeidah, according to the statement. Some of those provinces are in Houthi-controlled or contested territories.
The spokesperson said airstrikes between Sunday and Monday brought the total number of Saudi strikes and missile attacks to 3,939 since the fighting in Yemen escalated earlier this fall.

Saree's latest comments came after he claimed in another statement Monday that the Houthis had carried out new attacks against Saudi Arabian infrastructure, including a civilian airport, over the last 48 hours.
Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi airport, military assets

A spokesman for the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed Monday that the group had carried out new attacks over the preceding 48 hours on Saudi Arabian infrastructure, including a civilian airport.

Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesman, said in a statement shared on social media that the group had struck Saudi Arabia's eastern Dammam Airport "using two drones, and the operation achieved its objective successfully, resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport."
He said another drone hit an "early warning radar in Jizan," a city on Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast, while unspecified Houthi weapons hit "a military transport aircraft at Jizan Airport."

The Houthis have peppered Saudi Arabia's airports and energy infrastructure for weeks in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of Yemen's government in the impoverished Middle Eastern nation's grueling decade-long civil war. Iran has long backed the Houthis as a powerful proxy force, particularly as a counter to Iran's arch-foe Saudi Arabia, which shares a long border with Yemen.
Houthi drone and missile strikes last month , and despite the kingdom's vast military and financial advantage over the rebels, it .
There was no immediate information from Saudi officials to confirm or deny Saree's claims on Monday.
Senior Iranian official thanks Putin, talks "strategic cooperation" in phone call with Russian leader

The secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Monday, Iranian state media reported, in a continuation of recent talks between the two countries about the situation in the Middle East.

During their call, Rezaei and Putin discussed regional and global affairs, focusing on West Asia and ongoing "strategic cooperation" between Iran and Russia, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency.

Iran and Russia have long been allies, and their relationship has been cemented during both the ongoing Russian assault on Ukraine, and the U.S. war with Iran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in October that Tehran's ties with Russia were closer than ever, at the time that Moscow was "doing very little, if anything, to help" Tehran amid the war.
According to Tasnim, Rezaei thanked Putin Monday for Russia's support.
Iran's top diplomat says negotiations "proceeding very intensively," but "everything depends on" U.S. side

Iran's top diplomat said Monday that negotiations with the U.S., via mediators, aimed at reaching an agreement to end the war have been "proceeding very intensively," but he added that "everything depends on Washington's political rationality," according to Iran's state news agency IRNA.
IRNA quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as reiterating that Tehran will not back down from its conditions for a deal to end the war and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Closed-door negotiations have taken place via mediators, primarily Qatar and Pakistan, and Iranian officials said earlier Monday that it would be up to the U.S. side to make a move and end the monthslong standoff sparked by the joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.

"If they choose honest diplomacy, we are ready to engage," IRNA quoted Araghchi as saying. "If they intend to deceive us and launch military operations, they will face a response more bitter and forceful than before."
Another tanker on fire near Strait of Hormuz after hitting sea mine, Iranian news agency claims

The Iranian Navy claimed Monday that another oil tanker had caught on fire after striking a sea mine near the eastern entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency, which is closely linked with Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The report cited the Navy as saying the unnamed vessel had struck a mine while attempting to use shipping lanes through the strait that Iran considers unauthorized and unsafe, but which the Trump administration and U.S. military have repeatedly claimed are free and open.
The tanker had switched off its navigation systems, Fars said, referring to a common practice by commercial vessels trying to obscure their movements in the region.
Tanker owners should take a lesson from the fate of vessels that violate Iran's rules by trying to transit the strait without authorization from Tehran, the report cited the navy as saying.

On Friday, despite repeated assurances from the U.S. that the southern shipping lanes through the strait are open and safe to navigate, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region in the month of October alone, a record high.
The Iranian regime said earlier Monday that 11 ships had "caught fire" in or near the Strait of Hormuz in the last nine days alone.
Iran says it proposed shorter 2-day implementation period for proposed peace deal with U.S.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran had presented Qatari mediators with a proposal to shorten the implementation period of a potential deal with the U.S. to just two days from seven.

In an interview with Al Jazeera, Araghchi said: "The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days."
The Iranian minister added, however, that Tehran's conditions for a deal to end the war remain the same.

The Islamic Republic regime has demanded that the U.S. release frozen Iranian financial assets, lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports, as well as sanctions, and cease hostilities on all fronts, including Israel's battle with Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza. In exchange, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping traffic and commit to further talks on its nuclear program.
Under the original seven-day implementation proposed by Tehran, the Strait of Hormuz would have been reopened on the sixth day.

With the shortened implementation period, according to a statement on the Iranian government website, "a series of measures will be taken by the United States on the first day, and on the second day, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and maritime traffic will return to its previous conditions."
Iran claims 11 tankers "caught fire" in 9 days as U.S. commander declared Strait of Hormuz "free and clear"

Iran's government-run broadcaster IRIB said Monday that 11 oil tankers had "caught fire" in the Strait of Hormuz in the previous nine days, disputing U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper's assertion last week that "all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear."
In a post on X, IRIB said the 11 tankers had caught on fire since Oct. 25, the day on which it claimed Cooper made his recent fly-over of the strait.
The Iranian network offered no evidence, but claimed some of the vessels sank "to the depths of the sea."

Since the start of the war in February, Iran has targeted vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz in an effort to assert control over the narrow waterway, through which about a fifth of the world's crude oil supply typically passed prior to the conflict.
Cooper said last week in a Friday video statement that he saw no Iranian navy vessels in the strait during his flyover earlier in the week.
Later Friday, however, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the month of October alone, a record high.

The U.S. military and President Trump have repeatedly declared Iran's navy destroyed and insisted that southern shipping lanes through the strait are available to merchant vessels, but ongoing Iranian threats and attacks have kept the risks and costs for shippers high, which has helped Tehran keep maintain pressure on global energy prices.
Iran again warns of natural gas shortages ahead of winter
Iranian officials repeated warnings Monday of possible gas shortages for residents ahead of the winter, and they called on people to conserve the resource.
First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said he had to be honest about the stability of Iran's gas network in the colder months, as he asked the public to help conserve it.
Aref cited "imbalances accumulated over previous years and war-related damages," and warned that prices would increase for consumers who fail to conserve.
It is not the first time an Iranian official has warned about shortages. On , Iran's parliament speaker said natural gas consumption across Iran had to be reduced by 10%.

Iran's economy has been devastated by years of international sanctions, and the U.S. turn to economic warfare after the initial bombing campaigns of the ongoing conflict have strained finances for Tehran even further. The regime has not shown any willingness to bend on its demands to end the war, however, despite the economic pain for most Iranians.
Iran says the "ball is in the U.S. court" on any prospective peace deal
Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said Monday that the next move in the standoff with the United States is for President Trump to make.
"The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran's demands are reasonable and logical," Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists in Tehran.

Baqaei said ongoing negotiations, which have been brokered by Qatar, Pakistan and other mediators, were centered around the a seven-day proposal that Iran originally presented to the U.S. side in September, which calls for frozen Iranian assets to be released, the U.S. naval blockade to be lifted and an end to fighting on all fronts, in exchange for the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and further negotiations on other topics.

President Trump rejected the initial proposal, but both sides have since exchanged revisions, and Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he just needs to make a decision on whether to launch new attacks on Iran, or to make a deal to end the war.
Speaking Sunday to a radio network ahead of a campaign rally in Iowa, Mr. Trump said he would finish with the war soon, "one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he said, without offering any further context.
Netanyahu reportedly pushes for new U.S. strikes on Iran
President Trump told reporters Sunday that he'd spoken with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday and had a "very good talk with him."
Mr. Trump gave no details but said the two had discussed the war in Iran.
According to sources cited by Axios, Netanyahu pushed for Mr. Trump to strike Iran but the president wants to let the negotiations play out.
The U.S. and Iran both engaged in indirect talks via mediators led by Qatar who are pushing to strike a deal between both sides before the conflict escalated.
Mr. Trump has repeatedly hinted he is considering resuming attacks on Iran after the midterm elections.
Push for U.S.-Iran deal shadowed by threats to resume fighting

Qatari mediators are leading indirect talks aimed at reaching a deal between the U.S. and Iran, but the closed-door negotiations have been punctuated by exchanges of threats between the leaders of both countries.

Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz soon, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who added the outcome depends on answers provided by the United States.

On Saturday, President Trump said the U.S. still had to "take care of" one or two more potential targets in Iran, citing a suspected nuclear complex at Pickaxe Mountain. On Sunday he reiterated the threat, saying he may have to give Tehran "the hammer" at some unspecified time.

Meanwhile, Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei warned on Saturday there would be no "geographical limitations" should the fighting with the U.S. resume, adding that there is a "vast theatre" to inflict damage.
Both sides have previously acknowledged that indirect talks are underway but consistently exchange threats.
CBS/AFP
UAE hopes for diplomacy but braces for "the worst"

The United Arab Emirates' presidential adviser said Sunday that his country hopes a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations is possible, but that they are also preparing for the possibility of escalation.
Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Anwar Gargash said Iran's attacks on Gulf countries such as the UAE made this a "watershed year" for the region.

"We don't really want to see another round of confrontation in the region," Gargash told the audience. But he added that his country and the region are braced for the "the worst," referring to the resumption of active hostilities.

The UAE was consistently targeted by Tehran in the opening weeks of the war in retribution for U.S. strikes on Iran, disrupting tourism and daily life, and effectively throwing the security landscape of the region into question.
CBS/AP
Vessel struck in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. maritime agency says
A vessel was struck on Sunday by "an unknown projectile" in the Strait of Hormuz, a British maritime security agency said, after Qatari media reported an earlier attack on a gas tanker.
Britain's UKMTO maritime agency said "the master of a merchant vessel has relayed a mayday call... stating that another vessel has been struck by an unknown projectile" in the strait.

Earlier, Qatar's state news agency said a Qatari gas tanker had been attacked on Friday with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters. None of the crew members onboard the vessel were injured, and there was no environmental impact from the attack, the report said.
The attack struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, which belongs to the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said.
Since the Middle East war began in February, Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf in an effort to assert control over shipping.
Trump says war in Iran will be put away "very soon, one way or the other"
President Trump said he believes the U.S. will soon put the war with Iran away, "one way or the other."
The president was speaking to Right Side Broadcasting Network before a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday.
"We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other," Mr. Trump said. "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it… The job we've done is amazing."
Earlier Sunday, Iran's top diplomat said he hopes there is "rationality" on the U.S. side as diplomatic efforts seek to avert a return to all-out war.

articles.headline: MLB proposes new salary cap plan after free agency started on Monday night
keyFacts: Major League Baseball proposed postponing its new salary cap until the 2028 season instead of 2027, according to reporter Jeff Passan.
Passan reported that the updated proposal raises the proposed 2028 salary cap to $258.2 million and the floor to $180.2 million.
The Major League Baseball Players Union is expected to reject any proposal that includes a salary cap.
body: The 2026-2027 Major League Baseball offseason is finally underway, as free agency officially opened on Monday, November 2.

But there is one looming issue impacting all free agent negotiations right now: a potential lockout and salary cap for the 2027 season. As MLB tries to implement a salary cap, its latest proposal features a significant change from its initial proposal.

ESPN's Jeff Passan shared the latest on MLB's new CBA proposal, which reveals their salary cap plan won't go into effect in 2027, but rather start in 2028 to give teams time to figure out this offseason's free agency period without worrying about a cap. But that's not the only change to their salary cap proposal.
MLB proposes new salary cap plan with 2028 start date, new cap and floors

"Major League Baseball proposed postponing the implementation of a salary cap until the 2028 season while still putting into place the other elements of its labor offer for 2027, citing the difficulty of teams navigating free agency amid the current uncertainty," Passan shared.
This is a huge change in plans for MLB's CBA proposal, as instead of a salary cap instantly being implemented, they're willing to not have it kick in until the 2028 MLB season.
But that's not all the new MLB proposal changed. Initially, MLB's CBA proposal revealed a $171.2 million floor and a $245.3 million ceiling.
Passan revealed that those numbers changed. "MLB also set new numbers for its proposed cap and floor in 2028. The cap would be $258.2 million while the floor would be $180.2 million."

MLB's latest proposal still features a salary cap, but the key difference is that it wouldn't go into place until 2028, and that the floor is $9 million higher and the ceiling is $12.9 million higher than their initial proposal.

So, as baseball heads for a lockout in December, MLB's new CBA proposal raised the cap and floor while pushing the implementation of a cap until the 2028 season. It's a notable change from their prior proposal, as it's three major changes that favor the players.

However, the MLB Players Union (MLBPA) is likely to shut down any and all proposals from MLB that include a salary cap of any kind. Even though MLB changed some of its proposals, this likely won't be accepted by the MLBPA this offseason.

But this is still a notable update in this CBA negotiation, as MLB is already adjusting its asks to try and get a salary cap implemented, raising the floor and ceiling while giving teams an extra year to prepare for a salary cap.

keyFacts: The United Kingdom's Royal Navy is facing a severe state of readiness and lack of investment, leaving its attack submarines largely nonoperational and its surface warships overstretched.
French naval officials are meeting with European counterparts to address NATO security gaps caused by the declining condition of the British fleet.
Russia is exploiting these vulnerabilities by operating submarines aggressively in the Atlantic Ocean to threaten NATO interests and undersea cables.
body: The United Kingdom’s Royal Navy is globally regarded for the skill of its personnel, particularly its submariners. A capable navy has long been considered crucial to the security of this island country.
But not so today — at least not by U.K. politicians.

Today, the Royal Navy is in such a poor state of readiness that the entirety of its deployable force would struggle to defeat just three advanced Chinese warships . Things aren’t going to improve in the near future. Last week, the U.K. government kicked the can down the road on bolstering a woefully inadequate defense budget . This neglect of defense investment has been matched by all previous governments over the past 15 years. It has hollowed out a once-decisive capability.

Indeed, according to Defense Eye , the French Navy is meeting this week with its Spanish, Dutch, and Italian counterparts on a relevant matter: how to fill the NATO security gaps born of the Royal Navy’s decrepit situation. The problem is that these European navies also have limited ability to operate in the Arctic and Atlantic oceans due to their own governments’ failure to invest in defense. And while submarine forces from Germany, the Netherlands, and Norway are small but highly capable, they lack the endurance of their American, French, and British nuclear-powered counterparts.
Regardless, French concern over the Royal Navy’s status is certainly justified.

For a start, all of the U.K.’s attack submarines have been nonoperational for most of 2026 — one was deployed early this year. At the same time, the few deployable surface warships are heavily overstretched. This leaves the Atlantic Ocean vulnerable to Russian submarines that are seeking to threaten NATO interests. They include the Yasen-class attack and missile submarines, which are extremely quiet . As the Washington Examiner reported at the time , there is circumstantial evidence to suggest that one of these submarines was secretly operating off the site of the 2021 G-7 summit in the U.K. And in April, the Royal Navy was just barely able to counter Russian submarines that were targeting U.K. undersea cables.

Many senior U.S. Navy officers are probably thinking, “Thank goodness for the French, then.” After all, in a reversal of history, today’s French Navy is more agile than the Royal Navy. Following the start of the Iran war, France was able to surge numerous warships. The U.K. deployed only one destroyer, and only after a long delay in getting it out of port. That destroyer then broke down after arriving in the Mediterranean Sea and spent nearly two weeks undergoing repairs at a port in Crete. The U.K. attempts to deflect attention from this malaise by pointing to the deployments of its two aircraft carriers and ballistic missile submarines. But the aircraft carriers and their air wings have effectively zero anti-ship warfare capability. And the ballistic missile submarines are systems of nuclear deterrence, not conventional defense.

Russia is taking advantage of this dysfunction. Russian submarine forces are operating at Cold War levels and behaving as aggressively as they did then. And while the American and French navies can fill some of the gaps left by the Royal Navy’s submarine force, doing so places outsize burdens on their own readiness. This is particularly concerning from a U.S. perspective.
WHY TRUMP IS NOT GOING TO USE A NUCLEAR WEAPON AGAINST IRAN

Speaking earlier this year, the commander of U.S. Pacific forces, Adm. Sam Paparo, warned Congress that “we certainly don’t have enough attack submarines, and our trajectory is on the wrong side.” Paparo’s comments reflect the fact that attack submarines would be crucial in defeating any future Chinese attack on Taiwan. And that contingency is the paramount conventional U.S. national security concern . The naval inadequacy of the U.K., America’s closest ally, is thus undermining the special relationship.

Put simply, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government needs to get a grip. It needs to throw money at the Royal Navy, now. It needs to stop pretending that hard naval power can be built around cheap unmanned systems. And most of all, it needs to find a way to get, and keep, its attack submarines at sea.

articles.headline: Spencer Pratt claims chilling death threats forced him into $1,200-a-night luxury hotel
keyFacts: Former reality TV star Spencer Pratt stated that chilling death threats and break-ins during his campaign forced him to stay at a luxury hotel instead of his burnt Palisades home.
Pratt claimed the threats occurred because he was a Republican, prompting him to hire armed security professionals and SWAT officers to protect his family.
Pratt lost the primary election and claimed in a concession video that he possesses damning evidence against one of the Democratic candidates.
body: Former reality TV star Spencer Pratt isn’t running for Los Angeles mayor, but that didn’t stop him from making Election Day headlines about his campaign — revealing why he controversially holed up at the luxury Hotel Bel-Air while campaigning after losing his Palisades home in the devastating wildfire.

Pratt stayed at the ritzy Hotel Bel-Air during his campaign, where rooms reportedly start at more than $1,000 a night and the lavish Swan Lake Suite can run $8,090. A TMZ report unearthed the luxury digs just days after Pratt released a campaign video featuring wife Heidi Montag and their family touring an Airstream trailer on the charred lot where their Palisades home once stood.
“This is where I live,” Pratt declared in the video.
He insisted that the airstream trailer was real and not a prop, noting how much money and work he poured into getting the trailer installed at his burned property.
“I got a sump pump and permanent plumbing connecting it to the sewer, and was still waiting on LADWP to connect us to the grid,” he explained.

“Throughout the campaign, I endured numerous death threats, to the point where I had to hire full-time security,” Pratt said. “People were breaking into my lot in the Palisades and leaving notes on the airstream with white powder in them.”
All those threats and invasion of privacy, Pratt claimed, happened because he was a Republican.
Pratt had to hire SWAT officers for security detail and that a “lunatic” charged at his son while he was boogie-boarding in the ocean, he claimed in his social media post.

“So, I had to hire a second security detail for my family while I was away campaigning. I don’t know if you’ve ever had to hire 4-5 armed security professionals with blacked out SUVs, but…it’s not cheap,” Pratt said.

His Palisades lot was a “security nightmare,” he was told, and the Bel-Air, unlike other hotels, had actually good security settings. “The Hotel Bel Air is surrounded with a fortress wall, with a single point of ingress, a fatal funnel that takes you over a moat, just to enter the property,” the former candidate explained.
Pratt argued he would have had to book 3 extra rooms at any other place for extra security, which would have cost him $3,000 more per night.
Pratt ended with a tirade against what he called left-wing violence, recalling a campaign encounter with Raman in an elevator where he noticed she had no security.

“It was at that moment I realized the bubble the left lives in. We have a communist violence problem in America,” Pratt said. “Even they know, deep down, they never have to worry about violence because the violence only ever goes one way, and it comes from their team.”
Since Pratt lost the primary, the former star has continued to commentate on politics. He may also not be done with the mayoral race even after Election Day.

In a viral concession video posted months ago, he claimed he has damning evidence that would force one of the two Democrat candidates to resign and that he’ll release it when voters “pick their demon.”

articles.headline: How the Left cheapened human dignity
keyFacts: Author Steven Pinker argued in an essay that appeals to human dignity are subjective and fail to support heavyweight moral demands.
The author states that human dignity is frequently misused in contemporary political debates as a catch-all justification to shield policies from scrutiny.
The author argues that human dignity on its own has moral and political limits and does not dictate specific government policies.
body: The atheist public intellectual, Steven Pinker, penned an influential essay nearly 20 years ago titled “ The Stupidity of Dignity .” Pinker argues that appeals to human dignity are “squishy” and “subjective” and fail to support “the heavyweight moral demands assigned to it.” He prefers “autonomy” as an alternative.

Autonomy, however, is also subjective and squishy. Indeed, from a purely materialist atheistic perspective, we can’t coherently claim that autonomy exists because it’s not “matter.” Using autonomy to justify morality also means, unsettlingly, that babies, the elderly, the mentally and physically impaired, and, if we’re consistent, those who are asleep have little or no value because they are not fully autonomous.
Autonomy thus has trouble supporting the moral weight assigned to it, too.

Yet Pinker remains right that human dignity is often misused as a catch-all justification. Like “diversity,” “inclusion,” and “social justice,” appeals to dignity frequently assume that the meaning of the term is self-evident and that its very utterance establishes the moral supremacy of the position it’s advancing.
Pinker’s critique was aimed at dignity’s use in bioethics . However, invocations of dignity are also prominent in contemporary foreign policy and immigration debates.
Why, for example, is it wrong to question indiscriminately sending money to international NGOs? Because it’s an offense to human dignity.

Why should we never challenge the constitutionality of birth citizenship ? Because it’s an offense to human dignity (an “offense” currently committed by every country in Europe, none of which recognizes American-style birth citizenship).
Why must we remain silent about the harms caused by mass migration? Because it’s an offense against human dignity.
Why should the national census, which determines political representation, include illegal aliens? Because failing to do so, yes, is an offense against human dignity.
And how does dignity lead to these conclusions?
Because it does.

The tragedy is that human dignity, rightly defined, should form the foundation of the moral and political order. To recognize dignity is simply to affirm that all human beings have inherent and equal worth sheerly by virtue of being human.

Defined this way, human dignity generates two kinds of moral imperatives: a) negative prohibitions (things we should not do), and b) positive mandates (things we should do). What’s prohibited? Everything that, until recently, everyone in the West believed was wrong: murder, mutilation, abuse, torture, false imprisonment, theft, and exploitation. What’s mandated? Caring for those unable to care for themselves.

But here’s the crucial point: The only way to respect the negative prohibitions that human dignity generates is not to act — not to kill the innocent, not to mutilate, not to abuse, not to imprison without just cause, not to take what’s not yours, not to take advantage of others, etc.

What about the mandate to care for those in need? Like the negative prohibition, the moral imperative itself is categorical: All things being equal, we should take care of those who cannot care for themselves. Yet there is a crucial distinction. While there’s only one way to respect the negative prohibition on violating human dignity (not doing it), there are manifold ways to respect human dignity by providing aid.

A host of questions arise: Whose needs should I focus on and in what order of importance? What is the most effective method of giving assistance? What may appear to be helpful but is actually harmful? How can I provide aid in a way that does not cause an injustice to another, including my own family, community, and country? How can I be sure that the need is authentic and not fraudulent? How do I respond when those receiving aid appear to be taking advantage of it? How do I respond when those receiving aid are using it to cause harm to themselves or to others?

The complexity rises exponentially when the “I” becomes a “we” in the form of government policy, especially when recognizing that public expenditure to assist the needy comes from public funds — and public funds come from taxation, which is backed by the coercive power of the state. Respecting people’s dignity in the form of giving them something — especially if that something includes the benefits of citizenship — thus quickly becomes a highly contested political question, one that can be addressed only by wading through a sea of competing moral assertions based on an incomplete and often distorted understanding of the causes and effects of the problems we are seeking to address.
UN STRUGGLING TO PROTECT FOREIGN AID PROGRAMS FROM BAD ACTORS UNDER RUBIO AGREEMENTS, DOCUMENTS SHOW

The point is that, beyond the general imperative not to harm people and to do what’s possible to care for those in need, human dignity, by itself, does not have much to say about what we should and should not do in the political realm. This is not a criticism of human dignity. It is only a recognition of its moral and political limits.

To identify these limits, however, is to criticize those who engage in the rhetorical abuse of dignity, those who brazenly and carelessly toss it about in political discourse as both a weapon to advance their aims and as a shield from scrutiny. The end result — and I fear we’re already there — is that “dignity” loses both its rhetorical and moral force, fading into just another word partisans employ to get what they want.
Matthew Petrusek, Ph.D., is the senior director of the Word on Fire Institute and co-editor of Value & Vulnerability: An Interfaith Dialogue on Human Dignity.

articles.headline: 'Overwatch’s New Mythic Skin Shows Blizzard Is Finally Shaking Things Up
