body: Overwatch season 5's mid-season update is here, and with it comes quite a lot more than your typical mid-season update. Staples like Junkrat's Loot Hunt return, and it coincides with another round of the Excavation Initiative this time. There's a big end-of-season story event set in Rialto that caps off Vendetta's rise to (and recent fall from) power and locks some of its rewards behind a paid pass. And rather unexpectedly, there's also an Overwatch x Stellar Blade collaboration.
Overwatch's Eve Protocol crossover adds five skins from Shift Up's action game:
- Widowmaker as Eve
- DVa as Lily (with Toki designed after a late-game Stellar Blade boss)
- Freja as Raven
- Vendetta as Tachy
- Soldier 76 as Adam

The collaboration runs through Nov. 17. Like with most recent crossover events, the skins are all available in the shop only. There's no event that rewards you with a free skin from the collaboration.

Also in new skin news, the back half of the season sees Roadhog get his first Mythic skin, a fitting milestone to mark his popular revamp at the start of season 5. Roadhog's Mythic is, fittingly, Necrotic Knight. The base version Blizzard showed sees Roadhog clad in silver and toxic green armor with a mask sporting one of those plague doctor beaks. Doctors stashed herbs in those beaks in the middle ages, though something tells me what Roadhog has there is rather less wholesome and healthy. Anyway, the skin's later tiers give him scarlet armor decorated with ropes of jade and a big skull mask. It's pretty cool.

The story's big climactic event is Taking Reign, where Doomfist and Overwatch clash in Rialto. (Vendetta's presumably still in jail following the events of last week's flashy animated story.) Taking Reigh lasts for five weeks and has 24 tiers of rewards, though they're divided into a free track and a paid event track similar to how NetEase handles Marvel Rivals events. The free pass includes an epic Sigma skin recolor, and the paid one has Vendetta's new weapon and a legendary Doomfist skin. That track costs 1,000 Overwatch coins or roughly $10.

Blizzard's changing how Overwatch's competitive drives work this season, too, where you earn points by winning matches and lose points when you lose. Namely, drives aren't just competitive anymore. You can get your signature tag by playing in competitive mode, or you can stick to quick play to get legacy weapon points. Once you reach the fourth checkpoint in this season's drive, you can choose to equip certain signatures from previous seasons' drives if you want.

articles.headline: Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in
keyFacts: Apple released Siri Recap and Live Rewind in the developer beta for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
Siri Recap summarizes conversations into notes, while Live Rewind transcribes the last 15 seconds of audio.
Both opt-in features process data securely to address privacy concerns and can be enabled or disabled at any time.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Siri Recap and Live Rewind are now available to try in beta.
- Siri Recap summarizes your conversations into notes.
- Live Rewind transcribes the last 15 seconds.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind, Apple’s two controversial, always-listening Audio Intelligence features, are now available on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 with the iOS 27.3 developer beta. Both features are opt-in.

Apple unveiled Siri Recap and Live Rewind in September alongside its Series 12 and Ultra 4 smartwatches, but it waited to release the features until after the smartwatches launched. Siri Recap provides a high-level summary of meetings, while Live Rewind continuously records audio so the watch wearer can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds.
More from ZDNET
How Siri Recap takes conversation notes on Apple Watch
1. Look for Siri Recaps in the Siri app
Within the Siri app, users will find a new section called “Recaps,” where both the Siri Recaps and Live Rewinds live.

Siri Recap isn’t listening for nitty-gritty details within a meeting or recording a transcript’s worth of text. It’s more geared toward a conversation’s key takeaways, like important dates, times, prices, and action items. A demo of the feature showed an off-the-cuff conversation between a parent and a child discussing college application strategies. Siri Recap took notes on the high school activities the student could pursue to include in their application, the topics they could write about in their essay, and the colleges they could consider applying to.
2. Save Siri Recaps, export, or delete
After a conversation, a user can save the meeting notes in the Siri app or export them to Notes or Journal. If they don’t save the conversation, it’s automatically deleted after seven days.

Apple designed the feature to exclude certain information from the Siri Recap. It includes a person’s name only if they introduce themselves or if their name is regularly brought up in conversation. Otherwise, it avoids identifying speakers. It also scrubs the audio of language that promotes self-harm, financial and authentication data, and personal identifiers.
3. Enable or disable Siri Recaps at any time

You can enable or disable Recaps at any time through Control Center. You can create something akin to a Focus mode to automatically enable the feature once your Apple Watch detects you’ve reached your office or college lecture. Each morning, Siri Recap sends a notification to alert you that the feature is on. At the end of each day, you get a reminder to check your daily recaps in the Siri app.

The feature constantly assesses whether a conversation is relevant, optimizing its detection based on the conversation’s context, proximity, and length. It pauses summarization when a user is on a phone or FaceTime call, plays music, or uses earbuds. It won’t work when Bluetooth devices like AirPods are in use.
How Live Rewind records 15-second transcripts on Apple Watch
1. Double-press the Digital Crown

Double-press the Digital Crown to see a transcript of the past 15 seconds of conversation. The Apple Watch chimes and displays an animation to indicate it’s in use, then shows the transcript for 30 seconds.

Live Rewind is built for those head-in-the-clouds moments when you miss a tidbit of information and can’t go back and ask what a speaker said. I think about how useful this could be in a college lecture or boardroom setting, where dozens of people’s conversations and questions prevent someone from asking a clarifying question about what was discussed.
2. Share the Live Rewind snippet with Siri

The user can send the snippet to the Siri app to save it or ask about it (if they want to look up the definition of a mentioned term or get more information on the history of a mentioned topic, for example). If the user doesn’t act on it, the snippet is deleted. Any snippet you save is encrypted through iCloud. The audio buffer updates continuously, and unused audio is automatically deleted. It’s processed on the device and not sent to Apple.
How Apple Watch protects your audio

To some, an always-on, always-listening smartwatch can sound like a privacy breach waiting to happen. That’s a fair concern, and Apple has taken steps to address privacy and security concerns with its Secure Exclave.
The Secure Exclave explained

Think of the Secure Exclave as a private island on the S11 chip where the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 process audio. A secure audio buffer processes the raw audio, and a secure pairing mechanism privately enables the connection between a paired Apple Watch and iPhone.

For Siri Recap, the S11 chip listens to detect whether the watch wearer is part of a current conversation. Once detected, audio enters the Secure Exclave, where it’s encrypted and sent to the Secure Exclave on the iPhone. The iPhone turns that audio into condensed text, essentially editing the conversation to remove filler words or irrelevant information, and then it’s sent to private cloud compute. Private cloud compute creates a recap, delivered to your iPhone’s Siri app.
This process ensures that no one, including Apple, can access the audio data.
How to turn off Siri Recap and Live Rewind on Apple Watch
Don’t want your Apple Watch to listen to you? Siri Recap and Live Rewind are off by default, according to Apple.
If your Apple Watch prompts you to enable Audio Intelligence during setup, you can choose which features to turn on.

On its support page, Apple said you can “turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone.” Once it’s enabled, you can “turn it on or off at any time from Control Center.” To enable Live Rewind, Apple said to “open the Watch app, tap Siri, then tap Live Rewind and turn on ‘Double Click Digital Crown.’”
I haven’t tested these controls myself. I’d expect you can follow the same steps to switch Live Rewind off, but I haven’t confirmed that yet.

articles.headline: Siri Is Getting Ears on the Apple Watch: Here’s What That Means for Your Privacy
keyFacts: A new software beta rolling out for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 introduces audio intelligence features including Siri Rewind and Siri Recap.
Apple stated that raw audio is processed securely on the device chip and full transcripts are deleted before summaries are sent to the cloud.
Both new features are opt-in and require users to manually enable them during setup before they begin listening.
body: Your Apple Watch is about to start listening a little more closely (if you want it to). A beta rolling out this week gives Siri ears on the Series 12 and Ultra 4, with new features that can recall what was said in the last 15 seconds and summarize conversations throughout your day.
Faster Shazam and Sound Recognition for better accessibility

Audio Intelligence, as the new set of perks is called, consists of four audio-related features: music recognition, sound recognition, Siri rewind and Siri recap. The first two, which have been available since launch, include a faster Shazam that can recognize songs without even opening the app.

I’ve been testing it in beta and noticed it responds much faster, especially since I don’t even have to open the app to identify a song. Songs now appear automatically in my watch’s Smart Stack. This even includes the lullabies I sing to my toddler at bedtime, though understandably, it hasn’t been able to identify those.
Sound Recognition
Sound Recognition can alert people who are deaf or hard of hearing to sounds such as a crying baby, barking dog or doorbell.
How to access: You have to enable the feature on your iPhone, under Settings > Accessibility > Sound and Name Recognition and toggle it on. You can even select which sounds you want it to identify.

In my testing, it successfully identified my fake cough, the doorbell and the car horn. But then it spent the rest of the day gaslighting me, telling me there was a dog barking or a car honking when there clearly wasn’t, which made me question both my own reality and its listening range. But this may require further testing, since I’m still on the beta versions of all these.
The newest features, which are out now in beta, are the most controversial, and I’ll be testing them more this week.
Siri Rewind: Like Live Photos for audio snippets

At any point during the day, Siri Rewind lets you double-click the Digital Crown to pull up a text snippet of what was said in the previous 15 seconds, kind of like the audio version of Live Photos (which lets you see a few seconds of video before and after you pressed the shutter).

How to access the transcribed text? If you do nothing after seeing it on screen, it disappears. You can also ask Siri about it, or save it to the Siri app to view later on your phone. Old audio is continuously replaced by new audio and then deleted, so if you don’t trigger the feature to recall the last 15 seconds, it’s gone.

This is for unplanned moments where you need to revisit information without having to ask the speaker to repeat themselves. Apple’s keynote example showed someone reviewing the specials menu at a restaurant after the waiter had already walked away from the table. Whether you want to look away from the person speaking down at your watch instead of just asking them to repeat what they said is more of an etiquette question, but it could be helpful during large presentations.
Siri Recap: Automatically summarizes meetings and conversations

Siri Recap can listen in the background while enabled and generate high-level summaries and key points of conversations throughout your day. This can be anything from a parent-teacher conference or work meeting to spur-of-the-moment conversations or brainstorming sessions with coworkers that you wouldn’t go out of your way to record with Voice Memos.

How to access it: Similar to Siri Rewind, the notes from these recaps can either be saved in the Siri app and exported to the Notes or Journal app, or deleted. They automatically delete after seven days if you don’t delete manually.
Who controls when Siri’s listening?
Both features are opt-in, meaning you have to go out of your way to enable them during setup for them to work.
Once they’re on, Siri Rewind requires you to manually double-tap the digital crown to activate it. Siri Recap is completely customizable.

You can leave it on at all times and let Siri decide what counts as important conversations to recap, set it to on a schedule based on important meetings for the day, or enable it manually via the new Siri Recap icon in the Control Center on your Apple Watch like you would Focus mode or Do Not Disturb.

If you forget to turn it off, you’ll get a reminder in the morning telling you it’s on. You’ll also get reminders to check your recaps throughout the day and notifications when schedules start or stop, so you’re aware when it’s active.
And it won’t work for conference calls or FaceTime, if you have your AirPods or headphones in. It only works with audio it can pick up through the speaker.
What about battery impact?

Even if you do decide to leave all four on all day, Apple says they won’t ding your battery. The Apple Watch Series 12 gets around a day and a half of use (in my real-world testing), while the Ultra 4 gets anywhere from two and a half to three days of use.
This is possible because of Apple’s new S11 chip and its dual architecture in which one part handles background tasks without draining the more power-hungry main processor.
The looming privacy questions
The watch doesn’t save audio. It processes raw audio inside a hardware-isolated compartment on the S11 chip that Apple says even it can’t access, called the Secure Exclave.

Siri Recap doesn’t send a full transcript to the cloud, either. It condenses the text first, deletes the full transcript and sends only that condensed version to Private Cloud Compute. It omits financial data, authentication details, personal identifiers, language related to self-harm and government secrets.
The information pipeline for Siri Recap
- When enabled, the Watch detects when a conversation occurs.
- Audio enters the S11 Secure Exclave for on-device processing into condensed text, removing filler words for a high-level summary.
- Condensed text is encrypted and sent to Private Cloud Compute, where Apple says the data remains private.
- The recap is sent back to your iPhone and immediately deleted from Private Cloud Compute.
Apple makes a convincing case for how it’s protecting privacy, with security and accessibility innovations at its core.

Still, there’s something about explicitly giving the watch on my wrist the ability to listen to conversations that doesn’t sit right with me and many others. Especially when those conversations involve other people who may have no idea it’s happening.

There’s a chime that alerts people when Rewind is active, but to my knowledge, there’s no other warning when Siri is recapping a conversation. Smart glasses like the Meta Ray-Bans have an indicator light when they record video, though even that isn’t foolproof, since there are ways to get around it.

Maybe I’ll change my mind once I can actually test it. Apple has certainly given me reasons to trust how it protects data. I’m just not convinced yet that this is the intelligence I want my watch to have.
The features are rolling out in beta, with the update to iOS 27.3, initially in English, with additional languages planned later.
I’ll be testing over the coming weeks, so check back for more.

articles.headline: Silica, an FPS and RTS hybrid that mixes a smidge of Dune and Helldivers together, has left early access and entered 1.0
keyFacts: Developer Martin Melichárek and publisher Bohemia Interactive released the 1.0 version of Silica, leaving early access.
Silica is a sci-fi hybrid of first-person shooters and real-time strategy games set on an alien planet featuring warring factions and giant bugs.
The 1.0 update introduces the story-driven Centauri Campaign, 1v1 matchmaking, expanded Steam Workshop tools, and various improvements.
body: The concept of fusing an RTS and an FPS always sounds like a fun one, and since 2023 Martin Melichárek has been trying to make a new take on the combination under the watchful eye of DayZ devs Bohemia Interactive through Silica. Today marks the day that Silica leaves early access and enters 1.0, fully fleshing out its hybrid and mish mash of Dune's Arrakis and Helldivers' Terminids.

Digging into Silica a touch more deeply, it is a sci-fi shooter set on a planet where there's a fancy resource you're trying to mine that definitely isn't the spice. There are two warring factions competing for said resource, when, uh oh! Some bug-ish, giant aliens aren't very happy you're doing all that. So, you can either join the fray on the ground with some classic first-person shooting alongside your friends, or you can take the role of commander and dictate your artillery from above.

The 1.0 update obviously comes with a few additions, namely the Centauri Campaign, a "story-driven single-player experience set in the war for Baltarus. It opens with a cinematic intro and features fully voiced mission briefings and in-game dialogue. Between missions, a 3D planetary globe tracks the war as territory changes hands." Commanding your army should be a better experience now too, with the ability to "arrange units into formations, issue more precise movement and attack orders, and quickly select all units of the same type. Improved AI targeting and vehicle movement also help your armies operate more effectively in large-scale battles."

Beyond that, 1v1 matchmaking has been added in, where you can fight against another commander. The Steam Workshop sandbox tools have been expanded for building your own scenarios and sharing them with others. And there are a whole bunch of bug fixes, quality-of-life improvements and additions, and more. You can read about some of those in more detail in this handy little blog post. If you like what Silica is putting down, then you can pick it up on Steam.

articles.headline: Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
keyFacts: Apple released new always-on Audio Intelligence features in the watchOS 27.3 developer beta, including Siri Recap and Live Rewind.
Apple is also testing a redesigned Health app in the iOS 27.3 developer beta with expanded language support and new data tabs.
Apple stated that raw audio is processed within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and remains inaccessible to apps and the operating system.
body: Starting today, Siri can tune into the Apple Watch’s mic with Audio Intelligence features that are available in the new watchOS 27.3 developer beta rolling out now. The two new additions are Siri Recap, which uses “ambient listening” to generate summaries of your conversation, and Live Rewind, which generates text transcripts of the last 15 seconds of audio your watch’s mic detected.
Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
Audio Intelligence lets Siri ‘rewind’ and summarize audio from your Watch’s mic.

Apple is also releasing its redesigned Health app for testing today in the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and announced expanded language support in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese. It adds sections like a new Insights tab with summaries for heart, sleep, fitness, and other data that pop up during the day, a For You section with personalized recommendations, and health content like educational videos and articles.

- Live Rewind, which can help users recall what was just said in conversation. A double-press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so the user can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with. Users can ask Siri about the content of the text or save it to the Siri app to revisit later.

- Siri Recap, which can create high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment.
When it comes to the implications of an ambient, always-listening AI, Apple has released this Audio Intelligence

Privacy Overview (pdf) about how it plans to protect users’ privacy when their watch is listening around the clock. It goes into detail about Apple’s claims that users’ raw audio “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.” According to Apple, “If you use iCloud with two-factor authentication and have a device passcode, any Siri Recap summary or Live Rewind text snippet you choose to save syncs across your devices end-to-end encrypted in the Siri app.”

articles.headline: NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms
keyFacts: The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday for allegedly bypassing paywalls and selling copyrighted news content to AI companies.
The lawsuit alleged that Brave made over $100 million by copying and reselling publishers' work without permission to artificial intelligence firms.
Publishers accused Brave of direct and indirect copyright infringement, Digital Millennium Copyright Act violations, and blocking website advertisements while inserting its own.
body: The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies.

“Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere,” the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that “Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission,” while “publishers have received nothing.”

The lawsuit said, “AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index,” and use content from the Brave index “to train their own AI models” and “to respond to specific user queries.” The NYT lawsuit points to Brave’s website, which says the Brave Search API is “used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com.”

The lawsuit accused Brave of all the major types of copyright infringement: direct infringement, contributory infringement, and vicarious infringement. The lawsuit claims Brave infringes copyrights directly by scraping articles for its search index, for its “Ask Brave” AI search feature, and for the Brave API that “serves as an illicit source of unlicensed copyrighted material, including Times journalism, to other AI companies.”

The NYT accused Brave of being “a contributory and vicarious infringer when it deliberately induces, facilitates, controls, and profits from its users’ and GenAI customers’ copying of the copyrighted content.” Finally, the lawsuit said Brave violated the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) by circumventing technological measures the NYT and other content owners use to restrict access to their articles.

“The Brave Browser includes a default setting that, when activated, causes the browser to go behind website paywalls and provide the paywalled content to the user,” the lawsuit said. The browser “blocks advertising that would otherwise appear on The Times’s website, and instead shows its own ads, offering its users a cut of the revenue even as it deprives The Times of digital advertising revenue that helps it fund the expensive effort of producing journalism,” the lawsuit said.

articles.headline: Fortnite’s Plan To Survive GTA 6 Is Finally Revealed: Make Everything Free
keyFacts: Epic introduced a rare Item Shop Token in Fortnite's November mini-season that grants a limited number of players fourteen days of free shop items.
The promotion is intended to help combat the loss of players to the upcoming release of GTA 6.
Players who find the token must redeem it by December 15, 2026, and receive a second token to use in 2027.
body: Fortnite is a free-to-play game, but you probably already know that doesn't mean everything in Fortnite is free--not usually, anyway. But this month, pretty much everything in Fortnite's Item Shop will be free for a limited number of players and for a limited time.

As part of its new Treasure Hunters mini-season that began on November 1, players can find a rare in-game item that makes everything in the Item Shop free for 14 days, just in time for Epic to combat losing players to GTA 6 .

The Fortnite Item Shop Token grants those who find it something called Pirate Shop Access. Players can find the token in chests during any round of battle royale. Things like team size, Build or Zero Build modes, and ranked or unranked matches don't matter. In fact, playing in a squad is most beneficial; if a player finds the Item Shop Token, all their teammates in that round get it, too.

Once found, the Item Shop Token will make almost everything in Fortnite's shop free for 14 days. It must be redeemed by December 15, 2026, but anyone who finds the token also gets a second token for Pirate Shop Access to use in a future two-week window of their choosing in 2027.
Fortnite players are digging for gold in Epic's now-annual November mini-season.

Exceptions to the freebies include anything bought with real money, such as V-Bucks and some skin bundles, as well as battle-pass levels. You also can't claim more than one Sidekick (pets and other small characters that stay with you during rounds), and you can't gift items to other players for free either, as you may have guessed.

It may seem like a long list of exceptions, but Fortnite's Item Shop has grown to be massive in recent years. With 100+ songs perpetually available for $5 each, and dozens of emotes, skins, and other cosmetics cycling in every day, anyone lucky enough to claim a pair of tokens for themselves is in for a massive haul of stuff that would've cost hundreds, if not thousands, of dollars by the time their two weeks are up.

That second token is a clever way to extend the hype deeper into the post-GTA 6 world we're all about to live in starting on November 19, since this whole promo is clearly Epic's way of dealing with Rockstar's game. The most formidable threat to Fortnite's place atop the proverbial video game popularity mountain is nearly here. Epic needed something massive to keep players coming back, both in November and beyond. It felt like no collaboration, in-game event, or any of Fortnite's usual levers would be big enough on its own. But free everything? That'll help, at least.

Along with the early hype that accompanies any new season, plus the One Piece tie-in, Fortnite's battle royale modes are being played by about 2 million players during daytime US hours. That's about four times as many players as were playing on average in October. By giving it all the feeling of hitting the lottery, Epic is lapping up hype from Fortnite obsessives, casuals, and brand-new players alike.

Will it be enough to keep the hype going after Rockstar's future record-setter debuts? For many players, it won't be, but presumably some players will still carve out time for Fortnite in ways they wouldn't have before, even if only for a round or two before switching back to GTA 6.

Anecdotally, I'll tell you my son, who likes Fortnite but doesn't tend to play it weekly, spent much of last night researching strategies to find the Item Shop Token, then playing several rounds, reigniting a zeal for the game he hasn't had in a few years. He seems determined to min-max his chances at claiming one of the prizes for himself.

It's unclear how many players will win the prize, but until Epic turns that faucet off, he and others like him will be sprinting from chest to chest, hoping one of them bestows Fortnite's unprecedented GTA-countering prize.

articles.headline: UK's King Charles III decries 'monstrous injustice' of slave trade
keyFacts: UK King Charles III addressed the transatlantic slave trade's legacy at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda without apologizing or discussing reparations.
The monarch emphasized looking forward to address past injustices through future partnerships on healthcare, education, and climate protection.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham discussed potential debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and a new infrastructure investment for the Caribbean.
body: The United Kingdom's King Charles III on Tuesday opened this week's Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, a summit of 56 Commonwealth member-state leaders, by speaking of the tragic legacy of the transatlantic slave trade.
Charles told those gathered that he had furthered his "own understanding of the issues through listening, learning and looking."

"The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth. As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

The monarch stopped short of apologizing for Britain's role in the dark trade, as well as refraining from any talk of reparations. Instead, he spoke of the need to look forward when addressing the "monstrous injustice" of the past to insure that "evil need not have the last word."
Will the UK apologize for slavery, offer reparations?

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is also in attendance, has previously said that he could be open to an apology, and the run up to the summit has been dominated by talk of apologies and potential financial reparations.

Both the king and the prime minister have spoken of using the summit as an opportunity to address future partnerships by devising approaches to tackle healthcare, education and climate protection needs among those "who struggle against hardship and disadvantage" rather than dwelling on the past.
"We cannot change the actions of those who came before us," said the monarch as he opened Tuesday's session, "We can, however, learn from the past."

Burnham has said he would like to discuss debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations as well as announcing a €48.2 million ($54 million) investment into critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.
What was the British Empire's role in the transatlantic slave trade?

The British joined the institutionalized slave trade in the seventeenth century, and quickly eclipsed other European powers before involvement in the trade was outlawed for British subjects in the Slave Trade Act of 1807 and then done away with in the wider British Empire in the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833.

During that time, Britain outfitted almost one-third of all transatlantic slave voyages, facilitating the forced transport of over 3.2 million Africans, mainly to British colonies in the Caribbean and North America.
The Commonwealth of Nations consists largely of former British colonies whose combined GDP of roughly $14.5 trillion accounts for about 15% of the global economy.

articles.headline: Sony and Lionsgate Team up For Naruto Movie, Filming to Begin in Spring 2027
keyFacts: Sony and Lionsgate confirmed they are partnering on a live-action Naruto movie directed by Destin Daniel Cretton.
Lionsgate stated the film is targeting a production start date in spring 2027.
Lionsgate handles production and domestic distribution while Sony Pictures handles international distribution.
body: Sony and Lionsgate have teamed up for the live-action Naruto movie, which is targeting a spring 2027 start date.

Sony and Lionsgate have confirmed they will work together on Destin Daniel Cretton's live-action Naruto movie , with Lionsgate handling production and domestic distribution. Sony Pictures will handle international distribution. Lionsgate noted in a statement that Sony is a great partner for this specific project given its experience with anime and manga (Sony owns Crunchyroll, for instance).

“As a longtime fan of Naruto, I’ve always loved that beneath the extraordinary action is a story filled with heart, humor, and humanity," said director Destin Daniel Cretton. "Kishimoto-sensei created a world where unlikely heroes do extraordinary things, and that’s what makes it so special. Lionsgate has been an incredible partner, and I’m thrilled to reunite with the fantastic team at Sony. Together, we’re committed to capturing everything fans love about Naruto while introducing it to a whole new generation. I can’t wait for everyone to see what we’re creating.”

The Naruto movie has officially been greenlit by Lionsgate and is now barreling toward a production start date of spring 2027. As a result, we should hear more news on casting in the coming weeks and months. There's currently no confirmed cast for the film at the moment, but actor Charles Melton was reportedly in talks to play Kakashi back in August. Naruto will likely be one of the hottest projects in Hollywood ahead of its production start, with lots of younger actors likely trying to fight for a spot in the ensemble.

Destin Daniel Cretton just directed Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which grossed over $2.5 billion and became the third-highest-grossing film in history. Naturally, it makes sense that Sony would want to be involved with his next project, and it's likely other people in Hollywood will want to get on board as well. Cretton also did a bang-up job on Marvel's Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, which has given audiences more confidence in his Naruto movie.

Unfortunately, there isn't much precedent for great live-action adaptations of anime. Dragon Ball infamously got a live-action film known as Dragonball Evolution in 2009. It is genuinely awful and it may have scared Hollywood away from trying to adapt other anime after this. Maybe Naruto will crack the code, though.

articles.headline: GSMA warns of growing risks to mobile networks from extreme weather
keyFacts: The GSMA reported that extreme weather currently costs mobile operators $1.7 billion annually in repairs and warned that costs could reach $3 billion by 2050.
The report identified power supply failures as the greatest vulnerability for mobile networks during severe weather events like storms and floods.
The GSMA called on governments and regulators to collaborate with mobile operators to develop flexible resilience frameworks and maintain vital communications.
body: The GSMA wants governments and regulators to work more closely with mobile operators to help protect networks against growing risks from extreme weather.

As the global body representing the mobile network industry, the GSMA claims that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion annually to repair damage to cell radio sites, and it believes that figure could nearly double to more than $3 billion a year by 2050, under the climate conditions expected then.

The GSMA sets out its findings in a six-part research series, Futureproofing Connectivity: Climate Risk and Resilience in Telecommunications , alongside a separate document outlining its Policy Principles for Mobile Network Resilience .

The report identifies weather-related risks that can affect telecoms networks, along with the associated restoration costs. Towers, masts, and rooftop sites are particularly exposed to wind and storms or lightning, for example, while ground-level equipment at mobile sites can be inundated in flooding incidents.
High temperatures can cause radio equipment to overheat, while heavy rain can degrade wireless signal strength, and infrastructure in coastal locations may be exposed to storm surges.

However, the report fingers the electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability. If that gets knocked out, the network could go offline once any backup power is exhausted, which may take anywhere from a few hours to considerably longer, depending on the site.

Under current climate conditions, the cost of damage to cell sites is estimated at $1 billion associated with severe storms, while river and coastal floods account for $577 million and $124 million, respectively.
Based on projected mid-century climate conditions, the GSMA expects costs due to severe storms to rise significantly to about $2.37 billion, accounting for three-quarters of all damage.
The report asserts that cell network resilience requires a whole ecosystem approach, pointing out that if severe weather impacts power networks, then that also affects the telecoms infrastructure.

The GSMA says that network firms have traditionally managed the operational risks that may affect network availability, but claims they face barriers in conducting full assessments of those associated with climate change.

Some of these barriers are internal, such as lack of shared information between departments. Other barriers are in the different regulatory reporting frameworks, with infrastructure rules tending to focus on service continuity, while climate disclosure frameworks focus on governance, financial exposure, and reporting for investors and other stakeholders.
The report lists separate recommendations for network firms and for policymakers and regulators.

Operators are advised to embed resilience by design, using modeled projections for severe weather and future risk scenarios. They are also told to plan and test resilience across the wider ecosystem, engaging with others such as public authorities.

When it comes to policymakers and regulators, the report asks for resilience frameworks to be developed through consultation with the operators. It also advises coordination among mobile operators, electricity and fuel providers, and emergency services to help maintain vital communications during major disruptions.

And as if that isn't enough to chew over, the separate policy document sets out five principles for governments and regulators. These include avoiding prescriptive regulations and instead promoting outcome-based policies, encouraging dialog and consultation between governments, regulators, and operators, and developing resilience as a cross-sector responsibility.
“Mobile connectivity is essential infrastructure,” says GSMA Foundation president and chief regulatory officer John Giusti.
“Whether responding to extreme weather, power failures or other major disruptions, people, businesses and emergency services depend heavily on mobile networks,” he added.

“Severe weather is already costing the industry billions of dollars, and those costs are set to rise substantially. Building resilience will require a coordinated effort amongst operators, governments and the wider ecosystem.” ®

articles.headline: AOC campaign memo frames growth from progressive firebrand to national Democratic Party force
keyFacts: An internal strategy memo from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's campaign argues she has evolved into a national Democratic Party force focused on working-class voters.
The campaign memo highlights Ocasio-Cortez's fundraising totals of $38 million and her endorsements in competitive primary and general election races.
According to the document, Ocasio-Cortez launched a nationwide push centered on economic populism following the 2024 election of President Donald Trump.
body: An internal strategy memo released by the campaign committee for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N. Y.) and distributed to key allies makes the case that the lawmaker has evolved from a progressive firebrand into a formidable national political force.

The five-page document makes no mention of a potential 2028 presidential or Senate run. Instead, it urges stakeholders to view her record as that of one of the Democratic Party's most effective messengers for working-class voters.

Following President Donald Trump’s 2024 election victory, the memo states, Ocasio-Cortez launched an aggressive nationwide push to rebuild the party around economic populism and establish a broad movement for working families.
CARVILLE TORCHES DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS AS 'PACK OF FOOLS,' PRAISES AOC'S POLITICAL EVOLUTION

"Over the past two years, Rep. Ocasio-Cortez has built a record of success that extends beyond her own electoral victories," the memo reads. "The Congresswoman has emerged as one of the most powerful endorsements in the United States and New York State specifically. Candidates from rural districts and battleground seats see her as an asset for their general election campaigns."

The document highlights her fundraising reach, citing more than 2 million contributions totaling $38 million, an average donation of $17. 56, and over $3 million funneled to other Democratic candidates and state parties.
'SQUAD' RAKES IN RECORD $2.35M WHILE SLAMMING THE DOOR ON COP DONATIONS
Her small fundraising operation is unmatched in the House and rivals that of Sen. Bernie Sanders , I-Vt., the memo claims.

According to the document, Ocasio-Cortez’s strategy was shaped by post-2024 conversations with "Trump-AOC" split-ticket voters in her New York district, who expressed deep, cross-partisan frustration with a political establishment perceived as favoring corporate billionaires over ordinary workers.
BERNIE SANDERS ADMITS DEMOCRATS FAILED WORKING-CLASS VOTERS ON ECONOMICS, DRIVING THEM TO DONALD TRUMP

"As Democrats tried to understand why Trump had won again, Rep. Ocasio-Cortez argued that the path for the party to win back working class voters should be centered on economic populism, confronting concentrated wealth and power, and revitalizing American democracy," the memo states.

The memo points to race-altering endorsements in key primary and general election races across California, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Montana. It highlights Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign in Michigan and Sam Forstag’s Congressional primary victory in Montana as central case studies of her influence in rural and conservative-leaning areas.
AOC SIDES WITH BERNIE-BACKED PROGRESSIVE IN SENATE PRIMARY CLASH WITH SCHUMER ESTABLISHMENT

Forstag trailed significantly in the polls before joining Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders on stage at their "Fighting Oligarchy" rally in Missoula, Montana. Following her endorsement and appearance, he was able to erase the deficit and win the Democratic primary.

The document outlines a turning point following her unsuccessful bid for ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, alongside a March 2025 budget standoff in which Senate Democratic leadership accepted concessions during federal shutdown negotiations .
In response, Ocasio-Cortez shifted focus to taking her message directly to voters.
BERNIE SANDERS DISMISSES HALEY STEVENS, SAYS MICHIGAN RACE IS AGAINST THE 'BILLIONAIRE CLASS'
Speaking at a rally in Idaho, Ocasio-Cortez laid out the central thesis of her national tour:

"I want us all to understand that this constant pressure we feel in our lives—of the water rising up to our throats, the impossibility to afford anything easily, the fear of speaking up or being who we are in public, the bitter divisions driven more by online algorithms than the truth, the crumbling of our rights and protections— understand that this, right now, is what it feels like to be governed by billionaires," she said.
In the two years since, the memo states, Ocasio-Cortez has held large-scale rallies in purple, red, and blue places alike.
"She made race-changing endorsements in swing districts and deep-blue party primaries, as well as in her home base of New York City," the memo added.
